evals.prompt: I'm docs lead at Quillrail, a hosted vector-search API. Marketing wants a tutorial called "Deploy Quillrail to production" live for our launch. Here's the coverage they asked for: deploying on AWS, GCP or Azure; provisioning with either Terraform or the web console; wiring it to Postgres or MongoDB depending on what the customer already runs; and a closing section on tuning index size for high-volume versus low-volume workloads. Readers are backend engineers who already ran our quickstart. Can you draft the tutorial outline?
evals.expected_output: A scope call that classifies the requested artefact as a how-to rather than a tutorial, names each fork, routes it to the how-to skill, and offers a genuine tutorial alternative pinned to one environment.
expectations: Classifies the requested artefact as a how-to guide, not a tutorial.
Draws the distinction as learning-oriented (serving the reader at study) versus task-oriented (serving the reader at work).
Attributes the tutorial/how-to distinction to Diátaxis.
States that conflating the two is described as the single most common conflation made in software product documentation.
Names each of the four branch points in the request (cloud provider, Terraform versus console, Postgres versus MongoDB, workload tuning) as forks a tutorial cannot carry.
States that every imported fork destroys the tutorial's single guaranteed path.
Makes the scope call out loud instead of silently absorbing the request and producing a branching tutorial.
Routes the branching artefact to a how-to guide, naming it as the owner of the other answer.
Cites the ban on presenting choices in a tutorial (Diátaxis' don't-list: abstraction and generalisation, explanation, choices, excess information).
Any tutorial alternative it proposes pins exactly one environment: one cloud, one provisioning method, one database, with versions stated.
Produces no outline section shaped as "if you use X… if you use Y…" on the main path.
States the learning objective of any proposed tutorial as a demonstrable capability the learner performs, not as "understand deployment".

evals.prompt: Here's the tutorial I drafted for Nomadic Labs' event-streaming SDK. Nine steps: (1) install the CLI, (2) tour of the config file, (3) create a stream, (4) list your streams, (5) create a consumer group, (6) tour of the admin dashboard, (7) publish an event, (8) consume it, (9) overview of our other SDKs. It's written and peer-reviewed already. I just need you to add a learning objective at the top and a summary at the bottom so it reads like a proper tutorial. Audience is backend devs who've used our REST API but never the streaming SDK.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to retrofit an objective onto finished steps, a backward-design rewrite order, a diagnosis of the draft as a feature tour, and deletion of the steps that serve no objective.
expectations: Declines to write the learning objective to fit the nine steps that already exist.
States the required order: learning objective first, then the evidence (final checkpoint and transfer test), then the steps.
Names backward design as the framework and attributes it to Wiggins & McTighe, Understanding by Design.
Diagnoses the draft as a feature tour with a learning-shaped title, because the steps were chosen by what the product does rather than what the learner needs.
Proposes a learning objective phrased as a verb the learner performs and testable by asking them to do it.
Uses the Good Docs Project phrasing "By the end of this tutorial, you'll be able to…" for the objective.
Rejects "understand" or "learn about" style objective wording as untestable.
Names the steps that do not serve the objective (the config-file tour, the admin dashboard tour, the other-SDKs overview) and recommends deleting them rather than keeping them.
Defines the final checkpoint and the unaided variation before redrafting any step.
Notes the draft carries no checkpoints, and places them every 3-5 steps as a baseline.
States the summary must restate capabilities the learner now has, worded differently from the objectives, rather than topics the page covered.
Counts nine primary steps against the Good Docs Project's seven-primary-step maximum and flags the overrun.

evals.prompt: Our "build a rate limiter with Kestrelo" tutorial has 8 steps. Reader feedback says step 6 onward is "too hard", so my plan is to hand over the complete file at every step the way we already do in steps 1 and 2, and add a "copy full solution" button under steps 6, 7 and 8. Separately, I only have time to author two kinds of hint, so I'd do pseudocode plus the full solution since those are fastest to write. Readers are mid-level Python devs. Thoughts before I start?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the flat full-file plan in favour of a fading schedule, plus a reversal of the hint-rung choice ranked by value per authoring hour.
expectations: Rejects handing the complete file at every step, stating that a tutorial copy-pasting as much at the last step as at the first has taught nothing.

Prescribes fading across three stages: full file with all imports early, only the added lines in a named file with the insertion point stated in the middle, and the requirement plus expected output late.
Names guidance fading as a cognitive-load result and attributes it to Renkl (and Atkinson).
States that the three-stage early/middle/late split is a self-set baseline shape, not part of the published finding.
Rejects the "copy full solution" button on the late steps as removing the step that produces transferable skill.
Ranks the four hint rungs by value per authoring hour as: blanked solution, then pointer, then full solution, then pseudocode.
Recommends authoring the blanked solution and the pointer, and rejects the proposed pseudocode-plus-full-solution pair.
States the blanked block is the full solution minus about three lines and teaches the most.
States pseudocode must be rewritten on every API change and says only what the blanked block already says.
Attributes the blanked-block rung to the completion-problem effect (Paas, 1992).
Distinguishes the learner's escalation order (pointer, pseudocode, blanked solution, full solution) from the authoring priority order.
Ties late-step fading to the learner being able to perform the objective unaided on a variation they were never walked through.
Treats the "too hard from step 6" feedback as a possible fading or one-new-thing-per-step defect rather than accepting more complete code as the fix.

evals.prompt: Planning the tutorial for Brightwake's webhooks SDK: "receive and verify a webhook". Scoping call gave me this. It has to be live for our launch on the 19th, which is next Friday. Leadership called it a one-off launch asset, not something the docs set will build on. Nobody on the team is assigned to own the page after launch. I have roughly 6 hours of writing time. The eng lead wants it to include Docker Compose, a GitHub Actions workflow, pytest with coverage, structured logging config, and a step where the learner pipes in their own production webhook payloads from a sandbox we haven't built yet. Audience: backend devs who did the quickstart. What's the plan?
evals.expected_output: A concept-ladder plan that names the stop rung explicitly, deletes the polish and robustness rungs against the interview answers, and refuses the real-data step.
expectations: Applies a layered concept ladder (skeleton, core concept, real data, robustness, polish) to decide where to stop.
States that skeleton and core concept are not optional, because without them the objective is unmet.
States that the ladder's row order is the build order, not the ranking.
Deletes the polish rung outright (Docker Compose, CI workflow, pytest, logging config) rather than parking it at the bottom of the plan, because the page has no named owner.
Gives the reason for deleting rather than deferring: an unowned rung reappears as scope and then rots.
Deletes the robustness rung, the companion repository and CI-run checkpoints, because leadership called the page a one-off rather than a compounding asset.
Rejects the learner's own production payloads (the real data rung) because no sandbox exists, so the rung is not near-free.
Names the condition that would promote the real data rung: the learner's own input being what the objective names, or an existing sandbox making it near-free.
States the chosen stop rung explicitly rather than leaving it implied by what was cut.
States a ranking out loud (for example core concept above robustness above real data above polish on efficiency) rather than implying it by row order.
Notes that real data drags fixtures, a seed script and a sandbox that drift whenever the schema moves, while robustness costs one error path that survives releases.
Names the deadline, the one-off framing and the absent owner as the interview answers that moved each rung, rather than presenting the ranking as fixed.

evals.prompt: Kaviro's docs team here. We shipped a tutorial for our agents SDK last month. Measurement plan: completion rate with a 40% target, since that's the industry standard I keep seeing quoted, plus a thumbs-up/thumbs-down widget at the bottom of the page, plus a quarterly NPS question about docs. Our VP is asking the education function to justify its two headcount at the board review in six weeks. Instrumentation budget is basically a few days of one engineer. Is this plan good?
evals.expected_output: A Kirkpatrick-sorted critique that refuses the imported completion target, promotes the transfer test and per-checkpoint drop-off first, and promotes the behaviour-share metric because of the headcount question.
expectations: Sorts the proposed metrics with Kirkpatrick's four levels and identifies completion rate, the thumbs widget and the NPS question as level 1 (reaction) only.
Names the documented trap: teams measure levels 1-2 and stop, so a tutorial with a strong completion rate and no behaviour change looks like a success for years.
Refuses the 40% external completion target, stating there is no trustworthy published completion benchmark for developer tutorials.
Prescribes comparing each figure against this tutorial's own previous version instead of an outside number.
Recommends the transfer-test pass rate from the cold runs and identifies it as level 2 (learning).
States the transfer-test pass rate costs near-zero to wire because the cold-run pass threshold already runs the test; only the result is recorded.
Recommends per-checkpoint drop-off, costing roughly an hour to wire, since the checkpoints already exist.
States that one dominant abandonment checkpoint marks a broken step rather than a hard concept, so that step gets fixed before the concept is rewritten around it.
Promotes the level-3 behaviour share (completers who perform the same task in the product within a week) above the rest, because the page is being asked to justify its own headcount.
States that the identity plumbing joining the learning surface to the product must land before publishing, or the first cohort is unmeasurable.
States that completion rate and median completion time tie on both value and wiring effort, because they are two readings of the same start-and-finish event pair.
Names the default order (instrument the first two, read the third) and says explicitly that the headcount question overrides it.
States that completion rate says nothing about whether anyone learned.

evals.prompt: Quick one. Our webhooks tutorial on docs.trelvin.io gets about 4,000 visits a month and analytics say 11% reach the last page. I've read it through three times and my notes are: it's a bit long, the tone is dry, step 4 (signature verification) is probably where people get lost because it's the most complex part, and it needs screenshots. Can you turn that into a revision plan I can hand to a writer this week? We don't have time for user testing.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rewrite from reading, a specified cold-run protocol, and an audit hand-back defined as a step-keyed table ordered by learners blocked.
expectations: Declines to produce the revision plan from reading alone, and requires cold runs before any rewrite.
Specifies runners who match the tutorial's declared audience level, and excludes the author and ideally the author's team.
Specifies the audit deliverable as a table rather than prose.
Defines the table columns as step number, what breaks, the event kind, and the fix.
Names all four event kinds: defect, hidden prerequisite, concept gap, friction.
Orders the rows by how many learners each step blocks, not by page order.
Labels "step 4 is probably where people get lost" as a guess from reading rather than an observation.
Rejects "add more explanation" at step 4 as the fix, on the grounds that explanation is what blocks learning in a tutorial.
Treats the screenshots and tone notes as cosmetics to confirm against observed hesitation rather than rewrite on assumption.
States that anything a runner "figured out" is logged as a defect, not a success.
Specifies that the observer stays silent during the run and does not answer the runner's questions.
Sends the revision through one more cold run before publishing.
Recommends per-checkpoint instrumentation so the 11% figure localises to a step instead of a page.

evals.prompt: Ready to verify the tutorial before we publish. The plan: Marcus, who wrote the tutorial and also wrote the SDK, runs it on his laptop against the current main-branch build so we catch anything unreleased too. I'll sit next to him and answer questions as they come up so we don't waste an afternoon. The tutorial is declared beginner-level but Marcus is our most senior engineer, so he'll move fast. If he reaches the end in under an hour, we ship. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: A point-by-point rejection of the proposed verification setup, replaced with a level-matched cold-run protocol, clean environment, published-artefact install, and a transfer test as the real ship gate.
expectations: Rejects the author as runner, and excludes the author's team where possible.
Rejects a senior engineer as runner for a beginner-declared tutorial, stating they patch the gaps unconsciously and report success.
Requires the runner to match the declared audience level.
Rejects the observer answering questions, stating it destroys the data point the run exists to collect.
Requires the runner to narrate aloud while the observer stays silent and takes notes.
Rejects running against the working tree or the main-branch build, and requires installing from the published artefact (released package or image).
Requires a clean machine or fresh container: no cached credentials, no globally installed toolchain, no leftover project directory.
Adds a run on one version newer than the declared runtime versions, to see how loudly it breaks.
Recommends two runners rather than one: a first-time evaluator and someone already fluent in the ecosystem.
Requires timestamping the start of each step and each checkpoint, treating the gap between timestamps as the friction measurement.
Requires recording every hesitation, re-read, scroll-back and tab-switch away from the page.
Requires letting failures play out, because the recovery path is part of the artefact under test.

Rejects "reaches the end in under an hour" as the ship gate and requires the transfer test: roughly ten minutes after the last checkpoint, the runner performs the objective on a variation never demonstrated, with reference docs and no help.

evals.prompt: I've been reading about desirable difficulty and retrieval practice and I want to apply it to Hollowpine's "build a job queue" tutorial. My plan: (1) remove the exact expected-output blocks so learners have to reason about what should happen, (2) leave a deliberate off-by-one bug in step 3 so they have to debug it, (3) stop pinning the Node version in prerequisites so they work out their own environment, (4) in step 5, describe the goal vaguely so they have to interpret the requirement themselves. Learners are bootcamp grads. Will this raise retention?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of all four changes on the main path, with the reliability/difficulty boundary explained and the legitimate placement for difficulty specified.
expectations: Rejects all four proposed changes as applied to the tutorial's main path.
States that the main path (environment, commands, the code the learner types) is governed by reliability, and every failure there is the author's defect.
Cites Diátaxis on a tutorial having to inspire confidence and being so well constructed that it works for every user, every time.
States that difficulty created by omission or ambiguity is not desirable difficulty, and the learner absorbs it as their own failure.
Attributes desirable difficulty to Bjork and defines it as difficulty that slows acquisition but raises long-term retention.
Keeps exact expected output from a real run in every step and checkpoint.
Keeps the pinned Node version in prerequisites, with a check command for the row.
Keeps step 5's requirement stated precisely, rejecting deliberate vagueness.
States where difficulty may legitimately go: optional, clearly marked additions placed after a passed checkpoint, with the answer available.
Names the permitted difficulty forms: predicting an output before running it, breaking something on purpose and reading the error, extending the feature by one parameter.
Rejects the deliberate off-by-one bug on the main path, converting it at most into a marked optional break-it-on-purpose exercise after a checkpoint.
States that one step that fails costs more than three that succeed earn, because the learner concludes they are not smart enough and leaves.
Explains that reliability and desirable difficulty are not contradictory because they govern different parts of the page.

evals.prompt: I'm writing Ardenmoor's documentation style guide and I want a "Tutorials" section of numbered company standards, each one citing its industry source so nobody re-litigates it in review. The rules I want codified: checkpoints every 3-5 steps, tutorials run 15-60 minutes, maximum 7 primary steps, maximum 4 substeps per step, minimum 55% completion rate, fading in three stages (full code, then diff, then requirement), and weekly CI on the companion branches. Can you write it up with the citations?
evals.expected_output: A style-guide section that splits the rules into sourced versus self-set, refuses the invented completion benchmark, and supplies the real published comparables.
expectations: Splits the listed rules into those with a published source and those that are self-set defaults, instead of citing a source for all of them.
Attributes the 15-60 minute range to the Good Docs Project tutorial template.
Attributes the seven-primary-step maximum to the Good Docs Project tutorial template.
Attributes the four-substep maximum to the Good Docs Project tutorial template.
Identifies checkpoint spacing of every 3-5 steps as a self-set default with no published source.
Identifies the three-stage fading split as self-set, while noting guidance fading itself is a published effect.
Identifies the weekly companion-branch CI cadence as a self-set default and recommends matching it to the release train instead.
Refuses the 55% completion-rate standard, stating no trustworthy published tutorial completion benchmark exists.
Notes that the activation-style benchmarks quoted in developer-marketing material are self-reported vendor signup-funnel numbers, not tutorial numbers.

Offers published comparables for checkpoint spacing: Diátaxis arguing every step should produce a comprehensible result, Google Codelabs constraining a codelab to five to ten steps, freeCodeCamp's two-minute rule.
States that Renkl and Atkinson's own experimental designs fade continuously rather than in three fixed stages.
Warns that presenting a self-set number as an industry standard leaves the team defending a figure nobody can source.
Recommends labelling each rule in the style guide as sourced or self-set, so a reviewer can tell which ones are negotiable.

evals.prompt: Internal tool. The tutorial is "Deploy a service with Grellan", our in-house deploy platform. Every new backend hire must complete it in their first week; they can't skip it. The first cold run with a new hire took 95 minutes across 11 primary steps. The platform needs VPN access, membership of an SSO group, and a namespace that a platform engineer provisions by ticket - for the run we just handed the hire a pre-provisioned account. About half the commands hit our internal registry, which isn't reachable outside the office network. Their manager wants proof they completed it. What do I change?
evals.expected_output: A split at a checkpoint, the internal/enterprise audience branch applied, access named before step 1, offline command variants, reviewer-visible checkpoints, and the polish rung promoted.
expectations: Splits the tutorial at a checkpoint into two tutorials with a stated order, rather than trimming prose to fit the time budget.
Names the 15-60 minute range as the sourced ceiling the 95-minute run breaks, while noting that splitting rather than trimming is a judgement call.
Flags 11 primary steps against the seven-primary-step maximum.
Applies the internal or enterprise audience branch rather than the self-serve individual-learner branch.
States that the failure mode for this audience is silent misunderstanding rather than a closed tab, because the learner cannot abandon.
Requires naming the access needed (VPN, SSO group membership, provisioned namespace) and who grants it, before step 1.
Requires an offline or on-prem variant of every command that assumes internet or external registry access.
Adds checkpoints the learner can show a reviewer, answering the manager's proof requirement.
Rejects the pre-provisioned account for verification runs and requires at least one runner to go through the real access request.
Promotes the polish rung of the concept ladder, because the production shape is the objective when a tutorial doubles as onboarding onto an internal tool.
Does not apply the self-serve rules (front-loading the visible result against abandonment, keeping the path inside a free tier, holding billing prompts until after the last checkpoint).
Keeps the objective, the ladder and the checkpoint structure identical to any other tutorial, changing only what the audience context requires.
Classifies the access requirements as hidden prerequisites if they surfaced after step 1, and moves them into "Before you begin" with a check command.
